title: Paradigms of Interdependence
hook: A small broken promise can overdraw a relationship long before the argument begins.
counterintuition: Trust is built before the hard talk; the conversation only reveals the balance already there.
tryThisNow: Send one specific repair today: name the missed expectation, apologize without defense, and state the next observable promise.
keyTakeaway: Build interdependence by making trust deposits before you need trust; hard conversations spend the balance created by small reliable acts.

breakdown.fastRead:
A small broken promise can overdraw a bond long before the argument begins. A bond can look calm while the account is empty. Then one small withdrawal costs more than expected.

Shared work becomes possible only when free people build trust through deep listening, small courtesies, kept promises, clear aims, honesty, and sincere repair. Deposits are concrete: understand the person, keep promises, clarify aims, show loyalty, repair quickly.

Trust is not a mood; it is a balance changed by behavior.
breakdown.deepRead:
People do not hear the same sentence through high trust and low trust.

The public section starts by slowing the move toward other people. Self-mastery comes first because bonds expose private mismatch. A person who cannot keep promises internally will struggle to create dependable trust externally. The Emotional Bank Account supplies the operating metaphor. Every work with others deposits or withdraws from a bond's trust balance, and the balance changes how messages are received. With a high balance, mistakes are interpreted generously and talk remains flexible. With a low balance, even careful words are filtered through suspicion. Six deposits are named with practical specificity. Understanding the individual is first because a deposit must be meaningful to the receiver, not merely convenient to the giver. Attending to little things matters because small discourtesies often signal large disregard. Keeping promises is a major deposit because broken promises create deep withdrawals. Clarifying aims prevents the hidden contracts that later become resentment. Showing personal honesty includes loyalty to absent people, since present listeners learn whether their own reputation is safe. Sincere apology repairs withdrawals when it is specific and not repeated as a substitute for changed behavior. The section also reframes P problems as PC opportunities: a conflict, mistake, or disappointment can either deplete trust or build it, depending on how it is handled. The result is a bridge from independence to shared work through earned relational capacity.

The hard talk goes better when the account was funded before the room got tense.
breakdown.fullRead:
Trust behaves like a balance long before anyone names it. A promise kept, a private kindness, a clear expectation, and a sincere apology add weight. A broken commitment, a dismissive joke, a hidden agenda, and a careless assumption remove it. When the balance is high, people can survive mistakes. When it is low, even neutral words sound expensive.

The trust-account image gives public life a concrete measure. It does not reduce love or teamwork to bookkeeping. It shows that trust is built through conduct over time. Every small promise is either interest earned or debt added. Difficult cooperation needs that balance before the room gets tense.

Daniel coaches a middle school robotics team in Raleigh. At 5:10 p.m., his daughter asks him to see a small code fix while he is answering an important sponsor email. He almost says, later. Then he remembers that to her, attention is the deposit. He closes the laptop for four minutes, watches the robot turn, and asks one real question. The sponsor can wait. The child’s account could not.

Understanding the individual comes first because deposits are personal. One person feels cared for when given help. Another feels crowded. One employee values public praise. Another feels exposed by it. A deposit is not defined by the giver’s convenience. It is defined by the receiver’s sense of being seen.

Small courtesies matter because they tell people what to expect when stakes rise. Kindness at the door, attention during a story, and respect in disagreement all add quiet proof. Commitments matter even more. A promise is character made visible. Keeping it says, you can rely on me. Breaking it says, guard yourself.

Clarifying expectations protects both sides. Many withdrawals begin as invisible contracts. A manager expected a draft by Friday. The analyst thought Monday was fine. A parent expected help without asking. A child heard no request. Clear expectations turn resentment into agreement. Loyalty to the absent is another deposit. People trust someone more when they hear that absent people are treated fairly.

Apology is the repair move. A vague apology protects pride. A real one names the withdrawal and accepts the cost of repair. The limit is that deposits cannot be used as manipulation tokens. Trust is capacity, not leverage. The account exists so people can seek shared results without fear that every mistake will become a weapon.

examples.title: Parent Email

planSpec.stakes: a delayed reply may drain parent trust
planSpec.requiredBeat: make a trust deposit through clarity

examples.scenario: Maureen reads a parent email at 7:50 a.m. in Oakland. A bullying report from Monday still has no answer, and the parent is now copying the district. Before the bell rings, Maureen must decide: wait for every fact or acknowledge the delay, name the next check, and give a time for the follow-up.
examples.whatToDo: Maureen sends a brief status with the investigation step and a promised call time. She deposits clarity before asking the parent to stay patient.
examples.whyItMatters: Trust balances move before conflict peaks. A small kept commitment can keep a tense relationship solvent enough for harder facts later.

examples.title: Noise Repair

planSpec.stakes: one apology can prevent a feud
planSpec.requiredBeat: repair a withdrawal before defending intent

examples.scenario: Kenji meets his downstairs neighbor on the Vancouver stairwell at 8:05 p.m. The neighbor holds a phone recording of last night's chair scraping. Kenji wants to explain the moving boxes, but before the elevator arrives he has to choose between defending intent and repairing the disturbance the neighbor lived with.
examples.whatToDo: Kenji apologizes for the noise and offers felt pads that night. He can explain the move after he has first made a deposit against the withdrawal.
examples.whyItMatters: Intent does not erase impact in an Emotional Bank Account. Repair starts when the other person's experience is treated as real.

examples.title: Follow-Up Debt

planSpec.stakes: a missed call may cost a long relationship
planSpec.requiredBeat: pay back a broken promise with specific action

examples.scenario: Tara finds a reminder card under her keyboard at 9:18 a.m. in Bristol. She promised a factory buyer torque specs by Friday, and it is now Tuesday. Before sending a new quote, Tara must decide: pretend the delay is normal or name the missed promise and attach the exact specs.
examples.whatToDo: Tara opens with the missed commitment and sends the specs before discussing price. The repair is specific enough to start rebuilding credibility.
examples.whyItMatters: Broken promises accrue interest. A sincere apology without the promised substance leaves the account low; a named repair begins to restore trust.

examples.title: Cake Expectation

planSpec.stakes: unclear assumptions may disappoint a child

examples.scenario: Oscar picks up a birthday cake at 3:35 p.m. in Jersey City and sees vanilla frosting instead of the chocolate design his niece imagined. His sister says she thought he handled the order. Before the party starts, Oscar must decide: blame the bakery or clarify what each adult promised and fix what can be fixed.
examples.whatToDo: Oscar calls his sister, confirms the missing detail, and buys chocolate decorations nearby. He turns a vague expectation into a clear next step.
examples.whyItMatters: Many withdrawals come from assumptions no one checked. Clarifying expectations protects affection from preventable disappointment.

examples.title: Loan Trust

planSpec.stakes: a friend loan may strain the relationship
planSpec.requiredBeat: choose integrity over a convenient delay

examples.scenario: Celia sorts invoices in a Fresno garage workshop at 5:10 p.m. A friend loaned her money for a compressor, and the repayment date is tomorrow. Cash is tight, but she can pay half. Before dinner, Celia must decide: avoid the call or explain the shortfall with a date for the remaining amount.
examples.whatToDo: Celia calls before the deadline and sends the partial payment immediately. She treats transparency as part of repayment, not as an optional courtesy.
examples.whyItMatters: Integrity is a deposit because it reduces guessing. Even a hard update can strengthen trust when it arrives before the other person has to chase it.

examples.title: Ferry Answer

planSpec.stakes: small discourtesy may spoil public trust
planSpec.requiredBeat: make a simple courtesy deposit under pressure

examples.scenario: Andre hears a traveler ask the same fare question for the third time at 5:42 p.m. in the Halifax ferry terminal. The line is long and the printer jams. Before waving her aside, Andre has to decide if speed justifies a curt answer or whether a clear sentence will keep the line calmer.
examples.whatToDo: Andre answers the fare question once, slowly, while restarting the printer. He spends ten seconds on courtesy to avoid a larger trust withdrawal in the line.
examples.whyItMatters: Small courtesies are not soft extras in interdependence. They are deposits that make later impatience, limits, or bad news easier to bear.

questions.prompt: A manager receives a parent complaint after two days of silence about a bullying report. What deposit should happen first?
choices: Wait until every fact is known, because incomplete updates can create new questions and more parent anxiety.
Send a general apology without timing, since warmth matters more than procedural detail in a tense relationship.
Acknowledge the delay, name the next investigation step, and give a specific call time the parent can count on.
questions.explanation: A trust deposit can be small and specific. Clarity before completion keeps the relationship solvent enough for the harder conversation.

questions.prompt: An analyst tracing a failed partnership sees six missed follow-ups before the final argument. What does the Emotional Bank Account reveal?
choices: The argument created the trust problem by itself, so repair should focus on the last meeting.
Repeated small withdrawals lowered the balance before the visible conflict arrived.
The partners needed a better agenda, because structure usually outweighs trust in hard collaboration.
questions.explanation: The account metaphor exposes accumulated trust damage. Public conflict often becomes explosive because earlier promises and courtesies were spent down.

questions.prompt: A parent working on an urgent report hears a six-year-old interrupt for attention. Which response fits the relationship deposit logic?
choices: Attend to the child with respect and set a clear return point, treating the relationship as real work.
Tell the child the report matters more, then promise a longer conversation after the deadline.
Ignore the interruption quietly, since giving attention now would reward poor timing.
questions.explanation: The six-year-old scene tests whether efficiency outranks the relationship. A deposit may take little time and protect long-term trust.

questions.prompt: A director entering a merger talk wants to correct the other side's assumptions immediately. What capacity is missing if trust is low?
choices: A sharper slide deck, since clearer evidence usually replaces the need for relationship work.
A stronger opening demand, because uncertain trust requires showing firmness before courtesy.
Enough deposits for correction to be heard without becoming another withdrawal.
questions.explanation: Interdependence needs trust capacity before difficult production. Correction lands differently when the account is already low.

questions.prompt: A teacher apologizing for a missed student recommendation wants to restore trust. Which action is strongest?
choices: Offer a sincere apology and explain how crowded the week became for staff.
Name the missed promise, send the recommendation today, and give the student a copy of the submission.
Avoid mentioning the miss and complete the form quietly, since the result matters more than the error.
questions.explanation: The repair needs substance, not only regret. A kept replacement promise begins rebuilding credibility after the withdrawal.

questions.prompt: If you inherit a tense neighborhood dispute over noise, which move makes a deposit before debate?
choices: Acknowledge the disturbance they lived with and offer a concrete change before defending your side.
Explain your intent first, because neighbors should know the noise was not meant as disrespect.
Ask the neighbor to stop recording incidents, since recordings make cooperation feel adversarial.
questions.explanation: Intent does not cancel impact. A deposit starts by treating the other person's experience as real enough to repair.

questions.prompt: You are mediating a team that treats courtesy as a tactic to get cooperation later. What correction fits the hard edge?
choices: Courtesy should be used sparingly, because directness is usually more efficient than relationship deposits.
Courtesy is helpful mainly when disagreement is light; serious conflict depends on authority.
Courtesy matters because trust is production capacity, not a trick for extracting future agreement.
questions.explanation: The hard edge is capacity before production. Deposits are not decoration around teamwork; they make hard cooperation possible.

questions.prompt: Which action deposits trust when a friend loan repayment will be only half ready by the deadline?
choices: Wait until the full amount is ready, because partial payment may draw attention to the shortfall.
Call before the deadline, send the partial payment, and state the date for the remaining amount.
Send a casual text after the due date, since friendship should absorb brief financial pressure.
questions.explanation: Integrity lowers guessing. Early transparency and concrete payment protect the relationship better than silence or vague reassurance.

questions.prompt: Which move fits the Dag Hammarskjold spirit of serving one person when public recognition is absent?
choices: Give full attention to the person present, treating unseen service as a matter of integrity.
Choose the visible service task first, because public work creates stronger proof of commitment.
Serve privately only when the recipient can later confirm the effort to others.
questions.explanation: One-person service tests motive. The deposit is real even when no public credit follows it.

reviewCards.front: What is the Emotional Bank Account?
reviewCards.back: A trust balance in a relationship. Deposits build confidence and goodwill, while withdrawals create caution, resentment, or suspicion.

reviewCards.front: Why does understanding the individual come first?
reviewCards.back: A deposit counts only if it matters to that person. Good intentions can miss if they ignore the other person’s world.
They signal care in ordinary moments. Respect, kindness, and attention add trust before tension tests the relationship.

reviewCards.front: Why are commitments such large deposits or withdrawals?
reviewCards.back: Promises turn character into evidence. Keeping one builds confidence; breaking one teaches the other person to protect themselves.
It prevents invisible contracts. People cannot fairly meet standards that were never made clear.

reviewCards.front: Why does Public Victory depend on Private Victory?
reviewCards.back: Trust in public work rests on private reliability. Self-mastery makes cooperation safer when disagreement or correction arrives.

implementationPlan.title: Fund the Trust Account
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Treat each key relationship as a trust balance shaped by specific conduct. The framework is Understand, Courtesy, Commitment, Expectation, Repair.

ifThenPlans.context: If someone rejects what you meant as help
ifThenPlans.plan: If the gesture misses, then ask what would count as support to them before trying again.

ifThenPlans.context: If you make a promise in a busy moment
ifThenPlans.plan: If the commitment leaves your mouth, then record it immediately and set the next action.
If expectations were vague, then clarify the result and deadline before treating it as defiance.
If trust is damaged, then apologize specifically and make one repair that costs real convenience.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one strained relationship. Make one deposit the other person would recognize, and clarify one expectation that has been assumed too long.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Review three relationships each week. Identify one deposit, one possible withdrawal, and one promise that must be kept before the next hard conversation.
